choose-the-right-source.title: Choose the right source for each claim

sections.title: Your assistant knows your tastes—but not tonight’s menu
sections.content:
You have a clear request from Module 1. Now imagine the assistant suggests a dish that was removed last week. The missing capability is grounding: connecting a claim to information that supports it.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) means retrieving relevant material and supplying it to a model before it answers. In our project, a menu description can support what a dish contains. A live quote is needed for the current total. A cached description cannot establish either availability or the final price.

sections.alt: Menu cards are filtered before a source and freshness check.
sections.caption: Find relevant evidence, filter constraints, then verify what is current.

sections.question: A cached menu lists a dish at $16. What can you safely conclude?

options.text: The cached source lists a $16 item price; current charges need checking.
The dish must still be available.

sections.explanation: A description supports a bounded historical claim, not current stock or a final checkout quote.

sections.title: Give evidence an address and a date
sections.content:
Attach a source identifier, an item identifier, and a checked time to evidence. “Menu A, item tofu-bowl, checked at 18:05” is more inspectable than “I read it somewhere.” A timestamp helps you reason about freshness; it is not a guarantee.

Separate relatively stable descriptions from fast-changing stock and charges. Our lab uses fictional, fixed records and marks stale ones. In a real product, define how long each source may be reused and recheck before a consequential action.

sections.question: Match each claim to its best evidence.
sections.explanation: Different claims require different sources; one generic context dump cannot replace them.

sections.title: Make uncertainty visible in the recommendation
sections.content:
A useful recommendation can say: “This menu describes a tofu bowl at $16. I have not verified the current checkout total.” That is a narrower and more useful claim than “This will definitely arrive for $20.”

The Retrieval Lab implements filtering and ranking over sample data. It does not run an embedding model or a generative model. You will inspect which record supports each result before adding those components. Background: retrieving context with its meaning intact.

sections.question: Write a recommendation when the menu is known but the final charge is not.
sections.sample_answer: The menu describes a tofu bowl for $16. It matches the stated preference, but I need a current fee and availability check before confirming it fits the all-in budget.
sections.explanation: Compare your reasoning with the sample. A different wording is fine if it preserves the decision and the evidence behind it.

chunk-and-retrieve.title: Keep meaning intact when you retrieve

sections.title: A useful sentence can become misleading when cut apart
sections.content:
Suppose a menu says “Peanut noodles: contains peanuts. Tofu rice bowl: no peanut ingredient listed; shared kitchen.” A poor split can separate a dish name from its warning. Chunking divides documents into searchable pieces while preserving enough context to understand each piece.

For this small menu, use one complete item record as a chunk: name, description, tags, source, and freshness. Do not join a warning to a different dish just because it is nearby in the source.

sections.question: How should you chunk a small menu for this prototype?

options.text: Cut every 20 characters, even through item names.
Keep each item with its description, metadata, and caveats.
Merge every restaurant into a single paragraph.

sections.explanation: An item-level record preserves the meaning needed to interpret a candidate.

sections.title: Similarity finds candidates, not truth
sections.content:
An embedding represents text as numbers that can be compared for semantic similarity. Keyword search matches terms; semantic retrieval can connect related wording. Neither proves that a dish satisfies a dietary requirement.

Hybrid retrieval combines lexical and semantic signals. A reranker reorders retrieved candidates using another relevance assessment. Add either when measured misses justify the extra complexity. The lab’s transparent keyword score gives us an inspectable baseline, not a disguised embedding model.

sections.question: Match the retrieval component to its job.

pairs.right: Reorder a candidate set by relevance

sections.explanation: Retrieval components choose evidence; constraint checks still decide whether it is suitable.

sections.title: Inspect retrieval before blaming the answer
sections.content:
If the right item never reached the answer stage, rewriting the answer prompt may not fix the problem. Inspect the query, candidate records, exclusions, and final context.

Try “tofu” versus “plant based” in the lab. A keyword mismatch is an observable limitation. You can add a small synonym rule as a learning exercise, then discuss when semantic retrieval would generalize better. Keep the dietary filter independent of the relevance score.

sections.question: The answer omitted the right tofu dish. What do you inspect first?
sections.sample_answer: Check whether the item was retrieved, whether its record preserved the relevant description, and whether a filter excluded it correctly before changing the answer prompt.

sections.title: The best-looking result may be unacceptable
sections.content:
A spicy chicken bowl may match the query better than a tofu bowl. If vegetarian is a hard requirement, the chicken bowl should never win. Separate eligibility from ranking.

For our fictional dataset, first exclude unavailable, stale, non-matching dietary, or over-budget items. Then rank eligible items using query relevance. A preference score must not buy its way past a hard constraint.

sections.question: A non-vegetarian dish has the highest relevance score. What should happen?

options.text: It wins because relevance summarizes everything.
It is excluded before eligible dishes are ranked.
It is shown as vegetarian with a warning afterward.

sections.explanation: Hard requirements define eligibility; ranking only compares candidates that pass.

sections.title: Calculate a total with explicit assumptions
sections.content:
The lab adds item price, delivery, fees, tax, and the chosen tip in integer cents. That avoids simple decimal rounding surprises and makes the calculation easy to audit. These values are training fixtures, not current charges.

The user’s “under $25” means strictly less than 2500 cents. “At most $25” would permit equality. Preserve that distinction rather than changing it silently. Unknown charges cannot be treated as zero in a real checkout calculation.

sections.sentence: For a strict “under $25” limit, the total must be less than ___ cents.
sections.explanation: There are 100 cents in a dollar. Equality does not satisfy the word under.

sections.title: Explain why an item was excluded
sections.content:
The lab lists exclusions as well as results. “Outside the budget” and “unavailable” point to different next actions. When nothing qualifies, ask whether a preference can change; do not silently relax a hard requirement.

Dietary tags in a sample dataset are not a guarantee about real preparation or cross-contact. If a user reports an allergy, avoid inferring safety from a missing ingredient and require appropriate verification before presenting a safe-food claim.

sections.question: No sample item satisfies the current constraints. How should the assistant respond?
sections.sample_answer: Explain that no current candidate qualifies, show the limiting constraint, and ask whether the user wants to change a preference or revise the budget. Do not alter it without consent.
sections.explanation: Compare your reasoning with the sample. A different wording is fine if it preserves the decision and the evidence behind it.

build-grounded-shortlist.title: Build a shortlist with inspectable evidence

sections.title: Turn a list into a defensible recommendation
sections.content:
A useful shortlist needs more than three names. For each item, show why it fits, the sample total, and the supporting source. If two choices are close, explain the tradeoff: a better cuisine match versus a lower total.

Start with a deterministic explanation derived from the filtered record. Later, a model can improve wording while remaining bounded by the same evidence. Never let polished prose add an unsupported delivery promise.

sections.question: What belongs beside a recommended item?

options.text: A confident adjective and a stock photo.
Its source, explicit total assumptions, and reason it fits.
A promise that every dietary need is guaranteed.

sections.explanation: A recommendation should be inspectable and limited to what its evidence supports.

sections.title: Change one behavior in the starter
sections.content:
Open the lab bundle and find searchMenu in builder-core.mjs. Read the eligibility checks before the scoring function. Predict what happens when you change a search weight, then run the lab again.

Keep a counterexample: a highly relevant unavailable dish. If that dish appears after your change, you changed more than ranking. Restore the boundary check and rerun the case. A successful code edit should preserve earlier guarantees.

sections.statement: Changing ranking weights should allow an unavailable item to become eligible.
sections.explanation: Ranking weights should only reorder already eligible candidates.

sections.title: Carry the shortlist into the next module
sections.content:
Choose an eligible item, then open the Workflow Lab. The project now has two separate stages: obtaining defensible candidates and drafting a cart. This separation makes errors easier to locate.

Your completion artifact is a three-case evidence log: one successful search, one empty result, and one excluded stale record. Include both expected and actual behavior. These become regression cases in Module 5.

sections.question: Describe a regression test for your shortlist edit.
sections.sample_answer: Include an unavailable item with the strongest keyword match. After changing ranking weights, assert that it remains excluded while eligible items may change order.
